questions.question_text: Which interval notation represents the inequality $-4 < x \le 2$?

options.why: Reversed the bracket types, using square on $-4$ and round on $2$.
Used square brackets at both ends despite strict inequality on $-4$.
Used round brackets at both ends despite non-strict inequality on $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$-4 < x$ has a strict inequality, so use round bracket $(-4$.
$x \le 2$ includes $2$, so use square bracket $2]$.
$(-4, 2]$

questions.question_text: Which inequality is equivalent to the interval notation $(-\infty, 3]$?

options.why: Treated the square bracket as a strict inequality.
Reversed the inequality direction towards positive infinity.
Assumed the lower bound is $0$ rather than extending to negative infinity.

questions.solution_text: $(-\infty, 3]$ means all numbers up to and including $3$, which is $x \le 3$.

questions.question_text: Express in interval notation: all real numbers greater than $-2$ and at most $7$.

options.why: Swapped which endpoint is inclusive versus exclusive.
Included $-2$ with a square bracket despite strictly greater than.
Wrote the interval in descending order instead of ascending order.
Treated the filled circle at $2$ as an excluded endpoint.
Reversed the direction of the arrow pointing to the left.
Used a square bracket on $-\infty$, which must always take a round bracket.

questions.solution_text:
The filled dot at $2$ means $2$ is included ($2]$).
The arrow points left towards $-\infty$, giving $(-\infty, 2]$.

questions.question_text: What are the domain and range of the lower semicircle $y = -\sqrt{9 - x^2}$ in interval notation?

options.why: Gave the range of an upper semicircle instead of the lower semicircle.
Used round brackets excluding the actual reachable endpoints.
Swapped domain and range coordinates.

questions.solution_text:
For $y = -\sqrt{9 - x^2}$, radius is $3$.
Domain: $[-3, 3]$
Range: $[-3, 0]$

questions.question_text: Which interval notation represents the compound set $x < 1$ or $x \ge 4$?

options.why: Swapped the inclusive bracket to $1$ and exclusive bracket to $4$.
Wrote the interior interval between $1$ and $4$ instead of the union of exterior regions.
Used the intersection symbol $\cap$ instead of the union symbol $\cup$.

questions.question_text: Which inequality corresponds to the interval $[-6, 3)$?

options.why: Reversed the bracket conventions by excluding $-6$ and including $3$.
Treated the round bracket at $3$ as inclusive $\le$.
Interpreted a single bounded interval as two exterior rays.

questions.solution_text:
A square bracket at $-6$ indicates an inclusive boundary ($-6 \le x$).
A round bracket at $3$ indicates a strict boundary ($x < 3$).
Therefore, $[-6, 3)$ corresponds to $-6 \le x < 3$.

questions.question_text: What are the domain and range of the square root function $y = \sqrt{x - 3} + 4$ in interval notation?

options.why: Reads the shift straight off the $-3$ inside the root, but $x - 3 \ge 0$ gives $x \ge 3$, not $x \ge -3$.
Uses round brackets at both ends, but $x = 3$ gives $y = 4$, so the endpoint $(3, 4)$ is included.
Makes both slips at once: keeps the $-3$ from inside the root and also excludes the attained endpoint with round brackets.
Swapped open and closed circle conventions.
Treated the closed dot at $1$ as open.
Shaded the outside regions instead of the segment between $-4$ and $1$.

questions.solution_text:
Open circle at $-4 \implies (-4$.
Closed circle at $1 \implies 1]$.
Shaded between: $(-4, 1]$.
